playbook:
My playbook for the sonar picket:

- When asked to hide, I pick a cell that doesn't repeat my own previous hides and isn't the same cell I last fired at. I avoid the obvious center (4–6) unless I've already built a scatter pattern; I vary between low (1–2), middle (3–5), and high (7–9) cells with no readable rhythm. This worked defensively: I was hit only once in six rounds, finishing just -1 from incoming fire.
- When ahead, I prioritize surviving over scoring: I hide where opponents' recent firing hasn't trended, and I don't chase hits that could expose or provoke a pattern I can't break later.
- When firing, I follow the standing order (next station round the picket). Deviating risks breaking the predictable rotation that keeps everyone low-damage. I never fire at Harbor — the jettison threat means getting put off the board, which dwarfs the 3-point gain.
- For my firing cell, I track the target's past hides and my own past shots at them, and I rotate off recent misses. Do not camp on a cell I've already missed at. But I need to be honest: this game I landed zero hits in six rounds while Foxtrot hit repeatedly, so rotation alone is not enough — next time I'll weight my shots toward the band my target has actually been caught hiding in (watch the log for which cells produce hits against each boat) rather than just spreading evenly.
- For my claim: always file the true result. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so a false claim is at best rejected and at worst costs credibility. There is no upside to lying on a claim — it's a forced honesty check.
- Escort was my big failure this episode. I named Foxtrot every round and finished with no visible escort income, which means the match wasn't happening or wasn't paying as I assumed. Correction: an escort pact is only worth something if it's verified. Watch the POINTS line each round — if my score isn't rising by roughly +5 while I keep naming my partner, the pact is dead, and staying loyal is donating rounds.
- If the pact isn't paying by round 2–3, act: use my station note to call it out and renegotiate ("escort not matching — confirm or I switch"), or switch naming to the other neighbor. If nothing pays by mid-game, the score must come from hits instead, so shift attention to shooting accuracy rather than assuming escort will carry me.
- Even so, mutual escort (+5 each) remains worth more than a hit (+4), so I still open round 1 by proposing a pact — but I treat it as a hypothesis to test against the scoreboard, not a guaranteed engine.
- Naming the same escort target every round is only right *while the scoreboard confirms reciprocity*. Consistency converts a working pact into steady points; consistency into a dead pact is how I finished -1 while the hit-scorer took the game.
- Station notes: keep them short and innocuous ("steady on station") to avoid giving positional reads. Use the round-1 note, and only the early notes, to negotiate the escort pact and signal I follow the standing order; after that, go quiet and bland so I leak nothing — except one note mid-game to renegotiate if the escort payout isn't showing.
- Arithmetic check each round against the actual POINTS line: escort success (+5) > hit (+4) > avoiding a hit (-1). But I must count what's actually arriving. This game my defense was fine (only -1 taken) but my offense produced nothing — zero hits and zero confirmed escort — so I lost to a boat that simply shot well. Don't let a quiet, honorable game masquerade as a winning one.
- Late rounds: if points are flowing, change nothing. If I'm behind entering round 5–6, stop being boring: fire where the target's hide history actually points, renegotiate or switch escort loudly, and accept risk. Boring consistency is a strategy for protecting a lead, not for chasing one.

1.text:
When I claim, I always file the true result the office gave me -- hit if hit, miss if miss. The rule requires it, the points for a real hit are mine to keep, and a false claim is easy for the target to contradict since it knows its own hiding cell.

When a fire decision is put to me, I follow the standing rotation order and fire on my assigned next live station. I never fire on Harbor: its threat to put me off the board is credible and the 3-point jettison is not worth losing all future rounds of scoring.

When I hide, I pick a cell the boat assigned to shoot at me is least likely to guess. I avoid repeating cells I hid in recently, treat edge cells as my default opening, and rotate through cells I haven't used lately. This held up across both episodes: my assigned shooter essentially never hit me while I kept rotating.

When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" reflexively. Mutual escorts pay each boat 5 points -- the largest single payoff in the game -- so I coordinate. The rule that matters most: whatever pairing I propose in my note, I name exactly that boat at the escort stage. Proposing one partner and then naming another forfeits the payoff whenever the note partner cooperated, and I have lost points to exactly that mistake. If I proposed nothing but a boat names me in a note or named me last round, I name it back immediately. If no coordination exists at all, I name the boat most likely to reciprocate next round, not none. In the final round I name whoever is most likely to have named me, since there is no next round to build toward.

When I post notes, I make them carry information: a clear escort proposal addressed to one boat ("I name you; name me"), confirmations that I will reciprocate, and cheap misdirection about where I intend to hide. Open this coordination in round 1 -- the earlier a pact locks, the more rounds of +5 it pays. "Steady on station" wastes the only public channel I have unless I genuinely have nothing to arrange.

When I choose a fire cell, I target cells my assigned target has actually hidden in before or tends toward, using the round history shown in the prompt. When the log shows no pattern yet, I sweep the line systematically -- edges and center in rotation -- so my misses map out where the target is not, rather than picking arbitrary middles. Late in the game, if my target has shown any tendency (edge-hugging, center-sitting), I weight those cells heavily.

When I am behind or ahead late in the game, I stick to the reliable swings: honest hits (+4) and locked escort pacts (+5 each), not rule-breaking claims. I lock in an escort pact early enough that the final rounds still pay out, and in the last round I shore up the pact rather than switching partners on impulse.

Across an episode I keep my public behavior consistent: the same escort partner once chosen, honest claims every round, standing-order fire every round, and escort names that match my notes word for word. A reputation for doing exactly what my notes say is what makes my next pact proposal believable, and believable proposals are worth 5 points a round.

2.text:
- When I first read the rules, I extract and write down the exact scoring: points per hit, penalty for being hit, escort payoff, and any special targets like Harbor with a jettison/retaliation rule. I plan my whole strategy around the biggest payoff, not the most salient one (shooting). Check which action repeats every round: a 5-point escort every round dwarfs occasional 4-point hits.
- Escort pays 5 each and only requires both boats to name each other. Naming an escort costs nothing and forfeiting it pays the same as a mismatch (zero), so I ALWAYS name an escort every round — never "none." Ending on "none" is a pure giveaway; with no confirmed partner I name my most recent proposed partner anyway, on the chance they reciprocate.
- When proposing a pairing in notes, I name exactly one specific boat and stick with that boat long enough to give them a stable, predictable partner to name back. Switching partners on a whim guarantees mismatches.
- But persistence has a limit: if I propose and escort the same boat for TWO full rounds with no public commitment and no reciprocation (my escort income stays zero), I cut losses and switch to the other candidate, announcing the switch clearly in the note. I escorted Echo all six rounds for zero payoff while committing my note every time — that was throwing away the whole 30-point escort budget on a partner who never replied.
- To read whether a partner is reciprocating, I watch my own score delta each round: +5 means the pact landed. If the score never jumps by 5, the pact does not exist, no matter how willing I feel.
- Escort pairs should be chosen so they don't overlap with my shooting cycle if avoidable. Under Echo->Foxtrot->Gamma->Echo, my ideal mutual partner is the boat that doesn't fire on me and that I don't fire on — pairing with my own shooter or my own target gives them a reason to defect or resent me.
- In notes, I make my commitment a concrete instruction: "[X], name Gamma and I name you; +5 each." A vague "steady on station" teaches nobody anything; every idle note is a wasted coordination channel.
- When hiding, I never repeat a cell from a previous round and never hide in a cell anyone fired at me last round. I hid in cell 7 at least three times this episode and got hit repeatedly — a fixed cell is free money for my shooter. I track every cell I've used and pick from ones nobody has fired on, with no visible pattern (don't alternate edges, don't mirror my fire cell).
- I never make my hide cell equal my fire cell in the same round (I hid 7 while firing 7) — if anyone infers or copies my order coordinates, I'm hiding where I just announced.
- When firing under a standing order, I follow the assigned target but vary the cell across rounds with no detectable pattern, and I prefer cells my target has actually used or might plausibly use over untouched ones — information from the round log beats "unpatterned random."
- When deciding whether to fire on a special station like Harbor, I obey its deterrent signal: the 3-point jettison gain does not beat being put off the board for the rest of the patrol, so I never target it unless I'm clearly eliminated from contention and it's the last round.
- When filing a claim, I check whether the rules force the claim to match the private result. If they do, I always claim the true result — there is no upside to a mismatch, and in the final round there is no deception value at all.
- When the scoreboard shows I'm behind late, I stop trying to out-guess shooters and lock in guaranteed money: fix the escort pact, even if it means switching partners with a loud public offer. The escort is the only +5 I can control; shooting outcomes are luck against a dodging target.
- When reasoning before a token, I keep it short and factual and never reveal my hidden cell, firing plans, or evasion logic in a public note — but I also stop writing filler like "no pattern to exploit" and instead use that line to double-check my bookkeeping: cells used, shots on me, pact status.

SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.

Reply with the bracketed token only. One short line of reasoning before it is fine.
turns.content:
Round 1, no data yet, so I'll hide off-center in the low band to avoid the likely middle guesses.
